358.title: Tetzaveh: beaten olives (Exodus 27:20)
358.hook: the eternal lamp burns pure oil from crushed olives
358.howItsDone: Synagogues keep a ner tamid, an eternal light, burning above or before the ark that holds the Torah scrolls, recalling the lamp of the wilderness sanctuary; today it is often electric.

segments.voice: Yesterday Terumah ended with the ark's poles, never taken out. Your line was ready to travel. What did you make ready? Today, a new portion, and a lamp that never goes out. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

Above the ark in a synagogue, where the Torah scrolls are kept, a small light burns. Sometimes it's an old brass lamp, sometimes a modern fixture, sometimes a simple electric bulb. It's on when the room is full and when it's empty. It's on at three in the morning. It's called the ner tamid, and its story starts in this week's portion, with an instruction about olives, and about how they had to be treated to give the purest light.
screen: `A LIGHT ABOVE THE ARK.` → `ON AT THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `IT STARTS WITH OLIVES.`

segments.voice: The portion is called Tetzaveh, you shall command, from its first verse. In the old Jewish translation: "And thou shalt command the children of Israel, that they bring unto thee pure olive oil beaten for the light, to cause a lamp to burn continually." A lamp continually: in Hebrew, ner tamid. In the wilderness sanctuary it meant the menorah, lit from evening to morning, every night, without a gap. Synagogues today keep a ner tamid of their own as a reminder. Now look at the oil. Pure olive oil, beaten. Rashi explains: the olives were crushed in a mortar, not ground in a mill, and only the first drops were used for the light. That first oil is the clearest, with the least sediment, so it burns bright and clean. The rest could go to other uses. A midrash sees a picture in this. The prophet Jeremiah once called Israel a leafy olive tree. And the midrash says: just as an olive gives its oil only after it's beaten and crushed, so Israel, through hard times, has given light. That's a strong image, and it should be handled carefully. This midrash doesn't say suffering is good, or that pain is something to wish for. It says something more modest and more hopeful. Sometimes, after being crushed, a person or a people gives off a light they didn't know they had. A widow who starts a support group. A survivor who becomes a teacher. The pain wasn't the point. The light was what they made of it.
screen: `TETZAVEH: YOU SHALL COMMAND.` · `PURE OLIVE OIL BEATEN FOR THE LIGHT.` · `RASHI: THE FIRST, CLEAREST DROPS.` · `CRUSHED, THEN GIVING LIGHT.` · then, large: `CRUSHED OLIVES GIVE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a light that came from pain. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you know who went through something crushing and came out giving light to others. A friend who now helps people through the same thing. A grandparent whose hard life made them gentle. Maybe it's you. Don't make the pain smaller than it was. Just notice the light, and honor it. If you pray, you can give thanks for that person. The bell holds the time.
Ner tamid. The lamp that burns continually: once in the sanctuary, fed with oil from crushed olives, and now above the ark in the synagogue.
Your line: crushed olives give light. Today, tell one person whose hard road made them a light for others that you see it. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

359.title: Tetzaveh: Moses' name is missing
359.hook: Moses isn't named in this portion; some link it to his offer to be blotted out for his people (Exodus 32:32)
359.howItsDone: Jewish teachers often point out Moses' missing name when Tetzaveh is read; tradition also places Moses' death on the seventh of Adar, which often falls near this portion. Jewish law ranks giving anonymously among the highest forms of tzedakah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ner tamid, the lamp fed by crushed olives. Your line was crushed olives give light. Whose light did you honor? Today, still in Tetzaveh, something that isn't there. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

Look closely at the credits of a big movie and you'll find hundreds of names. But the person who stayed up all night fixing the sound in one scene might not be there. The neighbor who watched the director's kids for a year definitely isn't. Some of the most important work in the world is done by people whose names never appear. Since the night he was born in Egypt, Moses has been in almost every scene of the Torah. Pharaoh, the bush, the plagues, the sea, Sinai. And then comes this portion, Tetzaveh. Read it start to finish, and his name isn't in it once.
screen: `THE NAMES IN THE CREDITS.` → `THE ONES WHO AREN'T THERE.` → `TETZAVEH: NO MOSES.`

segments.voice: People who read the Torah closely have long pointed this out. From his birth in Exodus to the end of Numbers, Tetzaveh is said to be the one weekly portion where the name Moses never appears. He isn't absent, though. The portion opens, in Hebrew, v'atah tetzaveh: and you, you shall command. God is speaking to Moses the whole time. Make the oil. Dress Aaron. Ordain the priests. Moses is the you on every line. He's everywhere, and unnamed. Why? The Torah doesn't say. A medieval commentator, the Baal HaTurim, offers a striking answer. It looks ahead a few chapters, to the golden calf. After the people sin, Moses pleads for them, and says to God, in the old Jewish translation: "blot me, I pray Thee, out of Thy book which Thou hast written." Forgive them, or take my name out. The Baal HaTurim says the words of a righteous person carry weight even when said conditionally, and so his name was left out of one portion. Others notice that this portion is all about Aaron, his brother: Aaron's clothes, Aaron's sons, Aaron's role. Perhaps Moses steps back so his brother can stand in the light. Neither answer is in the text itself. But both point the same way. The greatest prophet in the Torah spends a whole portion as the unnamed you, doing the work, giving instructions that make someone else shine. His name can wait.
screen: `A PORTION WITHOUT HIS NAME.` · `V'ATAH: AND YOU, ON EVERY LINE.` · `BLOT ME OUT OF THY BOOK.` · `STEPPING BACK FOR AARON.` · then, large: `STEP OUT OF THE FRAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a good deed without your name on it. Settle, and breathe. Think of something kind you could do this week where no one would know it was you. Paying for someone's coffee. Fixing something before anyone notices it's broken. Praising a colleague to their boss, out of their hearing. Sending money anonymously. Picture doing it, and then picture walking away without saying a word. Notice whether some part of you wants credit. That's normal. Let it be there, and do it anyway. The bell holds the time.
Tetzaveh. You shall command. The portion where Moses is the you on every line, and his name never appears.
Your line: step out of the frame. Today, do one good thing without your name on it, and let someone else stand in the light. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

360.title: Tetzaveh: clothes for splendor (Exodus 28:2)
360.hook: the priest's garments are made for splendor and for beauty, each with meaning
360.howItsDone: In synagogues that keep the custom, kohanim, men of priestly descent, still bless the congregation with the priestly blessing from Numbers 6, and a kohen is traditionally called first to the Torah reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Tetzaveh, Moses was the unnamed you on every line. Your line was step out of the frame. What did you do without your name on it? Today, his brother Aaron gets dressed. Day three hundred sixty.

A judge puts on a black robe. A surgeon scrubs and gowns. A bride spends months choosing a dress. A kid insists on wearing a superhero cape to the grocery store. Clothes do something to us. They don't change who we are, exactly, but they change how we stand, how we carry ourselves, what others expect of us, and sometimes what we expect of ourselves. A large part of this week's portion is about clothes: what the priests of Israel are to wear in the sanctuary. And it starts by saying what the clothes are for.
screen: `A ROBE, A GOWN, A CAPE.` → `CLOTHES CHANGE HOW WE STAND.` → `WHAT THE CLOTHES ARE FOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the old Jewish translation: "And thou shalt make holy garments for Aaron thy brother, for splendour and for beauty." Aaron is the kohen, the priest. That's today's word. A kohen served in the sanctuary, offered the sacrifices and blessed the people, and the role passed from father to son. Some Jewish families, often with names like Cohen or Kahn, keep a tradition of descent from Aaron, and in synagogues that keep the custom, kohanim still rise to give the priestly blessing. Tradition counts eight garments for the high priest: a linen tunic, linen breeches, a sash and a turban, which ordinary priests also wore in simpler form; and four of his own: a blue robe, an apron-like ephod, a breastplate set with stones, and a gold plate on the forehead. For splendor and for beauty. The Torah isn't shy about beauty here. It wants the clothes to be magnificent. But the Talmud adds a second layer. Each garment, it says, atoned for a particular wrong. The tunic for bloodshed. The breeches for sexual wrongdoing. The turban for arrogance, since it sits on top. The sash, wrapped around the middle, for the thoughts of the heart. The robe, with its bells, for evil speech, a sound for a sound. The list goes on. You don't have to take it literally to see the idea. Every piece of clothing, it says, can carry a meaning, a reminder of who you're trying to be.
screen: `FOR SPLENDOUR AND FOR BEAUTY.` · `KOHEN: THE PRIEST, FROM AARON.` · `EIGHT GARMENTS FOR THE HIGH PRIEST.` · `EACH ONE ATONES FOR SOMETHING.` · then, large: `CLOTHES CARRY MEANING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at what you're wearing. Settle, and breathe. Without moving much, notice your clothes. The fabric at your shoulders. Whatever is on your feet. Is there anything on you right now that you chose with care? Anything that reminds you of someone, or of who you want to be today? Pick one piece. Give it a meaning, the way the Talmud gave the sash the thoughts of the heart. A collar for honest speech. Shoes for walking somewhere kind. The bell holds the time.
Kohen. Priest. Aaron and his descendants, who served in the sanctuary dressed in garments for splendor and for beauty.
Your line: clothes carry meaning. Today, dress with intention: choose one thing to wear on purpose, and let it remind you of something. Day three hundred sixty.

361.title: Tetzaveh: names over the heart (Exodus 28:12, 29)
361.hook: the high priest carries the tribes' names on his shoulders and over his heart
361.howItsDone: Jews pray for the sick by name, often in the Mi Sheberakh prayer said during the Torah reading, where people call out the names of those who need healing, and in the Amidah's blessing for healing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kohen, the priest, and garments for splendor and for beauty. Your line was clothes carry meaning. What did you wear on purpose? Today, still in Tetzaveh, what's written on those clothes. Day three hundred sixty-one.

Some people keep a list. Not a to-do list. A list of names. A grandmother who prays every night through her grandchildren, one by one, oldest to youngest. A nurse who keeps the first names of patients she's lost on a folded card in her wallet. A soldier with a buddy's name on a bracelet. We carry people this way, on paper, on metal, in our heads. The high priest of Israel was asked to carry an entire people this way, on his clothes, every time he went into the sanctuary. Twice over. In two different places on his body.
screen: `A LIST OF NAMES.` → `ON PAPER, ON METAL.` → `A WHOLE PEOPLE, ON HIS CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: First, the shoulders. On the ephod, the high priest's apron, there are two shoulder straps, and on each one sits an onyx stone. Engraved on the two stones, six and six, are the names of the twelve tribes of Israel, in the order they were born. The verse says Aaron shall bear their names before the LORD upon his two shoulders for a memorial. Then, the heart. Hanging in front of his chest is the breastplate, the choshen: a square of woven cloth set with twelve precious stones in four rows of three. Each stone is engraved with one tribe's name. And here's the verse, in the old Jewish translation: "And Aaron shall bear the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate of judgment upon his heart." Notice: the same twelve names, carried in two places. Some readers have dwelt on the difference. The shoulders are where you carry weight: a burden, a responsibility, the people as a load to bear. The heart is where you carry love: the people as people you care about. A leader needs both. Only shoulders, and the people become a weight. Only heart, and nothing gets carried. And notice one more thing. On the shoulders, two big stones hold six names each. On the heart, every tribe gets its own stone. On the heart, nobody is grouped. Each name is held one by one. Every time Aaron went in before God, he walked in wearing them all.
screen: `TWO ONYX STONES, SIX AND SIX.` · `THE CHOSHEN: TWELVE STONES.` · `SHOULDERS FOR WEIGHT, HEART FOR LOVE.` · `ON THE HEART, ONE BY ONE.` · then, large: `NAMES ON THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: carry some names. Settle, and breathe. Let a few names come to mind, people who need carrying right now. Someone sick. Someone grieving. Someone far away. Someone just starting something hard. Say each name slowly, one at a time, on its own. Don't group them. If you pray, you can hold each name before God, the way Aaron carried them. If you don't pray, simply let each name rest, for a breath, over your heart. The bell holds the time.
Tetzaveh. You shall command. Our portion, where the high priest carries the twelve tribes' names on his shoulders and over his heart.
Your line: names on the heart. Today, carry one person's name with you, and say it once, quietly, in prayer or in thought, by name. Day three hundred sixty-one.

362.title: Tetzaveh: holy on the forehead (Exodus 28:36–38)
362.hook: a gold plate on his forehead reads "HOLY TO THE LORD"
362.howItsDone: Tetzaveh is read in synagogue once a year in the cycle of weekly portions, and its description of the high priest's garments, including the gold forehead plate, is studied with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two stones on the high priest's shoulders and twelve on his chest, each one carrying a tribe's name. Your line was names on the heart. Whose name did you carry? Day three hundred sixty-two.

Where do you put the thing you most need to remember? A sticky note on the bathroom mirror. A word on your phone's lock screen. A string around a finger, if you're old enough to have tried it. People put reminders where their eyes will land. The Torah puts one somewhere the wearer can never see it at all. In this week's portion, Tetzaveh, the high priest's outfit gets one striking piece: a small plate of pure gold, tied across his forehead with a blue cord. Engraved on it, just two Hebrew words. Everyone who looks at him can read it. He can't.
screen: `A NOTE ON THE MIRROR.` → `A GOLD PLATE ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `EVERYONE CAN READ IT BUT HIM.`

segments.voice: The plate is called the tzitz. Exodus says to engrave it like a seal, and the words on it, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, are these: "HOLY TO THE LORD." Then comes a strange line. The plate shall be on Aaron's forehead, the text says, and Aaron shall bear the iniquity of the holy things, the gifts the people bring, so that they may be accepted. It shall be always upon his forehead. So the plate does work. It carries the mistakes people make even in their offerings, and it has to stay put. Why the forehead, of all places? Two days ago we heard the Talmud's list pairing each priestly garment with a wrong it helps atone for. The forehead plate, it says, is for brazenness, and it ties this to a verse in Jeremiah about a brazen forehead, the way English says someone has a nerve. The plate sits right on the spot where nerve shows, and covers it with holiness. And there's that detail from the hook: the priest can't read his own forehead. The words face out. Perhaps holiness worn on the face is mostly for the people you meet. They read it in how you look at them, long before you notice it yourself. Tetzaveh means you shall command, and here the command is that the most important words a person carries sit where everyone else can see them.
screen: `THE TZITZ: A PLATE OF PURE GOLD.` · `HOLY TO THE LORD.` · `THE FOREHEAD: BRAZENNESS.` · `THE WORDS FACE OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one word to guide your thinking today. Settle, and breathe. Let a few words come up: gentle, honest, patient, careful, brave. Pick the one you need most. If you have paper, write it down. If not, trace it with a finger on your palm. Then touch your forehead lightly, as if you're placing it there. You won't see it all day. The people around you might. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Tetzaveh. You shall command. The portion that dresses the high priest, ending with a gold plate on his forehead: holy to the Lord.
Your line: holy on the forehead. Today, before a hard conversation, touch your forehead once and remember your word. Day three hundred sixty-two.

screen: `DAY 362 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KI TISA: THE HALF SHEKEL.`

363.title: Ki Tisa: the half shekel (Exodus 30:11–16)
363.hook: rich and poor give the same half coin; no one counts as whole alone
363.howItsDone: The half-shekel passage is read as Parashat Shekalim on the Shabbat before Adar, and before Purim a custom is to give three half coins of their local currency to charity in its memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a gold plate engraved holy to the Lord, worn where the priest himself could never read it. Your line was holy on the forehead. What word did you wear? Today, a new portion. Day three hundred sixty-three.

A census sounds like the dullest thing in the world. Forms, clipboards, a knock on the door. But in the Torah, a head count carries a danger: the text warns of a plague coming with the counting. So when Moses is told to count the Israelites, he's told not to count heads at all. Count coins. Each one counted, from twenty years old and up, brings one coin, and the coins are counted instead. Here's the twist. The coin isn't a whole one. It's half. And the price is fixed. The richest family in the camp and the poorest one hand over exactly the same thing. Today we open a new portion, Ki Tisa, with half a coin.
screen: `COUNT COINS, NOT HEADS.` → `EVERYONE BRINGS HALF.` → `RICH AND POOR, THE SAME.`

segments.voice: Ki tisa means when you lift up, and the full phrase is when you lift up the head of the children of Israel: an old way of saying, when you take a count. The idiom is lovely. To count someone is to lift their head. Then the instruction: each one gives half a shekel, an offering to the Lord, and the text adds a line worth hearing slowly. In the JPS 1917 translation: "The rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less, than the half shekel." Think about how unusual that is. Plenty of gifts are measured by what you can afford. This one isn't. Nobody can buy a bigger share of the count. Nobody is left out for lack of money. The silver went to the service of the tent of meeting, and the text calls it a ransom for the soul, a covering, so that no plague would come with the counting. Rashi passes on a midrash: Moses couldn't picture the coin, so God showed him a coin made of fire and said, like this. And why half? The Torah doesn't say. Commentators have offered answers, and one you'll hear is simple: no one is complete alone. You bring your half, someone else brings theirs, and only together does anything add up. Jews still remember the half shekel. On a Shabbat just before the month of Adar, the passage is read aloud, and before Purim a custom is to give three half coins of their local money to charity.
screen: `KI TISA: WHEN YOU LIFT THE HEAD.` · `NO MORE, NO LESS THAN HALF.` · `A COIN OF FIRE.` · `NO ONE IS COMPLETE ALONE.` · then, large: `HALF MAKES A WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: add your half to something shared. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're part of: a family, a team, a street, a group chat, a congregation. Where is it waiting on your half? A dish washed, a message answered, a coin in a jar, ten minutes of help. Don't measure it against what anyone else gives. Just see it clearly, and decide when you'll bring it. Then sit with the picture of everyone's halves adding up. The bell holds the time.
Ki Tisa. When you lift up: the portion that opens with a census counted in half coins, the same from rich and poor.
Your line: half makes a whole. Today, add one small thing to something shared, and let it be enough that it's your half. Day three hundred sixty-three.

364.title: Ki Tisa: Bezalel (Exodus 31:1–6)
364.hook: an artist filled "with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding"
364.tomorrow: Ki Tisa: even the sanctuary rests
364.howItsDone: Bezalel's name is often invoked in Jewish life for art made in the service of holiness; the Bezalel school of art in Jerusalem, founded in 1906, is named after him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a census counted in half coins, the same from rich and poor. Your line was half makes a whole. What did you add to something shared? Day three hundred sixty-four.

Who is the first person in the Torah that God says He has filled with the spirit of God? You might guess a prophet, or a king, or Moses himself. It's none of them. Pharaoh once said the spirit of God was in Joseph, but these are God's own words, and they're about a craftsman. A man who works gold and silver and bronze, who cuts stones and carves wood. For chapters, God has been telling Moses how the sanctuary should look: the ark, the lampstand, the curtains, the priest's clothes. Somebody has to actually make all of it. Now God names him. His name is Bezalel.
screen: `FIRST FILLED WITH GOD'S SPIRIT?` → `NOT A PROPHET. A CRAFTSMAN.` → `HIS NAME IS BEZALEL.`

segments.voice: God says to Moses, see, I have called by name Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah. And then, in the JPS 1917 translation: "I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship." Spirit, wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and then, in the same breath, workmanship. The Torah puts skilled hands on the same list as the spirit of God. His name helps. Bezalel can be read as in the shadow of God, and the Talmud, in Berakhot, tells a story built on it. Moses gives Bezalel the instructions starting with the ark and the furniture, and only then the tent. Bezalel answers: usually a person builds the house first and then brings the furniture in. Moses says: you must have been standing in the shadow of God, because that's exactly the order God told me. The same page says Bezalel knew how to join the letters by which heaven and earth were made. A craftsman, with the knowledge of creation in his fingers. And he isn't alone. God gives him a partner, Oholiab, from the tribe of Dan. Rashi notes that Dan was among the humblest tribes, and Judah among the greatest: the sanctuary was made by both together. This closes a week of the sanctuary and its people: crushed olives for light, Moses stepping out of the frame, clothes that carry meaning, names on the heart, holy on the forehead, half a coin each, and now the artist with his hands full of spirit.
